sections.html:
The answer turns on where the house sits and whether the bill is current or late. For every municipality except the City of Milwaukee, the Milwaukee County Treasurer takes delinquent taxes for 2024 and earlier years. Inside the City of Milwaukee, the City Treasurer handles current and delinquent taxes alike.

Valuation is a local job. Call your assessor about what the property is worth and your clerk about the bill. The county has 19 municipalities, 10 cities and 9 villages, and it is the only Wisconsin county that is fully incorporated, so every parcel lies inside a city or village and none in an unincorporated town.

Milwaukee County is Wisconsin's most populous and most densely populated county. The 2020 census counted 939,489 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 924,216, a decline of 1.6 percent. There are 429,425 housing units. Only 49.9 percent of households own, so about half rent. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $230,700, median gross rent is $1,101 a month, and 1,046 building permits were issued in 2025.

Buyers and title companies check a parcel for delinquent amounts before closing, so learn what the Treasurer's records show before you list.

Under the state's 2026 Guide for Property Owners, an installment payer owes the first half by January 31 and the second by July 31, unless the local government set another schedule. If the first installment isn't received within five working days after January 31, the full unpaid balance goes delinquent on February 1. A late payment later in the year makes the balance delinquent on the first of the next month.

Payment or penaltyRule
First installmentDue January 31
Second installmentDue July 31
Statewide interest on late tax1 percent per month, back to February 1
Milwaukee County delinquency charge18 percent per year
City of Milwaukee installment planTen months, interest free, bill over $100, first payment by January 31

Some counties add a further penalty of 1.5 percent per month, and an owner who never pays can lose the property.

sections.h2: Paying a City of Milwaukee bill
sections.html:
The City Treasurer takes payments by mail, drop box, phone or online. The office is at City Hall, Room 103, 200 East Wells Street, Milwaukee, WI 53202, with a customer service line at 414-286-2240. No cash is accepted.

  • By mail: send a check in the return envelope from your bill, and mail it early.
  • Drop boxes: two Market Street locations, inside City Hall at the Market Street entrance and outside the Municipal Building, stay open around the clock. The Broadway entrance box is available during building hours.
  • Online: pay by ACH from checking or savings, or by card with a 2.75 percent convenience fee ($3.00 minimum).
  • Installments: a ten-month, interest-free plan is open if the real estate bill is over $100 and you can make the first payment by January 31.

Special charges and assessments left unpaid by mid-November may be added to the tax bill. Those can't be appealed or negotiated.

sections.h2: Paying delinquent taxes to the County Treasurer
sections.html:
Delinquent bills can be paid online, by mail or in person at the Milwaukee County Courthouse. Online payments go through Value Payment Systems, which charges 2.55 percent for credit or debit cards and a flat $1.50 for e-checks. The county gets none of that fee.

The Treasurer's records show every unpaid delinquent tax, penalty and interest charge, and a parcel with nothing owed shows a zero balance. A payment made today might not post until the next business day. If an amount looks wrong, or you want a monthly payment plan, call (414) 278-4033.

Collection tools include payments, the Wisconsin Tax Refund Intercept (TRIP), foreclosure and a lawsuit against the individual. A parcel in bankruptcy can't be foreclosed or collected on except as federal bankruptcy law permits. Because of the 18 percent yearly charge, the Treasurer notes that paying fast costs less, and a home equity loan or a mortgage refinance may cover the bill.

Non-agricultural property is assessed at market value as of January 1, and each municipality must be within 10 percent of market value at least once every five years. If you think your value is wrong, begin with the assessor. Then go to the Open Book period, when the roll is open for examination. The Board of Review starts at least seven days after Open Book opens.

Tell the clerk, in writing or by voice, that you plan to object at least 48 hours before the first meeting. Then file the Objection Form for Real Property Assessment (PA-115A). It counts as filed if the clerk has it within the first two hours of that meeting. You may ask the board to waive the hearing and go directly to circuit court, but a granted waiver ends your right to claim an excessive assessment or appeal to the Department of Revenue, and a court action under section 70.47(13) must start within 90 days of the waiver notice.

Exemption disputes bypass the Board of Review. An owner contesting exempt status files a claim of unlawful tax with the municipality by January 31 of the year the tax is payable, under section 74.35. Your clerk can give you the meeting dates.

Look up the parcel before you list or accept an offer. Outside the City of Milwaukee, use the County Treasurer's online search or call (414) 278-4033. Inside the city, use the City Treasurer's resident access system or call 414-286-2240. Have the title company confirm payoff figures for this year, any delinquent years and special charges.

Unpaid taxes can end in in rem foreclosure, where title to a delinquent property moves under Wisconsin law. The county doesn't sell foreclosed properties for the back taxes. It sells them at fair market value like any other property. Lender foreclosure auctions are a separate matter, held by the Sheriff on Monday mornings, and the Sheriff advises buyers to check for delinquent taxes first.

If back taxes are what stands between you and a sale, a cash buyer can often close without waiting on a lender's appraisal, and the payoff comes out of the proceeds at closing.

The new owner should record the change with the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds. If the former owner's name remains on a city tax bill, the new owner should check the change-of-address box on the payment coupon so a refund check doesn't go to the previous owner. Report mailing address changes to the City Assessor at City Hall, Room 507.

faqs.q: Who do I pay if my Milwaukee County property taxes are delinquent?
faqs.a: Pay the Milwaukee County Treasurer, unless the house is in the City of Milwaukee, where the City Treasurer collects current and delinquent taxes. The county number is (414) 278-4033 and the city line is 414-286-2240.

faqs.q: What interest applies to late taxes in Milwaukee County?
faqs.a: The County Treasurer charges 18 percent per year in delinquency charges. State rules describe 1 percent per month back to February 1, with an extra 1.5 percent per month in some counties.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Milwaukee County?
faqs.a: Installment payers owe the first half by January 31 and the second by July 31, unless the local government set a different schedule. Miss the first installment by more than five working days and the whole balance is delinquent as of February 1.

faqs.q: Can I put delinquent taxes on a credit card?
faqs.a: Yes, online through Value Payment Systems. Cards carry a 2.55 percent fee and e-checks a flat $1.50. The county receives none of it.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal an assessment in Milwaukee County?
faqs.a: Notify the Board of Review clerk at least 48 hours before the first meeting, then file the PA-115A within the first two hours of that meeting. Call your clerk for exact dates, which differ by municipality.
